title: The Built Environment and Spatial Form

findings.antecedent: houses built from mud (less permanent materials)
findings.consequent: fit between dwelling form and household composition
findings.mechanism: less permanent materials allow for easier adaptation to changing household needs
findings.quote: the fit is much closer in a society where the houses are built from mud as opposed to more permanent materials such as stone
Dwelling size may be an indicator of population size [with a proposed universal of 10 m²/person (262)]

findings.mechanism: rectangular forms are more permanent and easier to add onto, suiting sedentary lifestyles
findings.quote: Rectangular forms, which tend to be more permanent than round ones, have been found associated with sedentary societies (379)

findings.consequent: increased partitioning and monofunctional uses of spaces in built forms
findings.mechanism: specialization and stratification lead to differentiated uses of space, requiring more partitions
findings.quote: increasing social complexity in the form of specialization and stratification is expressed in the increased partitioning and monofunctional uses of spaces in built forms.

findings.mechanism: wealth allows for greater consumption of space and larger domestic groups
findings.quote: the houses of the wealthy are larger, not only because they consume more space per person but also because the domestic groups are larger (205, 264).

findings.antecedent: increasing participation in the capitalist system
findings.mechanism: modernization and capitalist integration lead to changes in housing and lifestyle that reduce neighborhood interaction
findings.quote: Increasing participa- tion in the capitalist system has also affected Greek housing (279), and the modernization of urban Japanese apartment plans has distanced neighborhood social relations (252).

findings.antecedent: developing countries modernize or become more westernized
findings.consequent: house styles representing collectivistic social relations and values
findings.mechanism: modernization shifts values from collective to individualistic, reflected in house styles
findings.quote: As developing countries modernize or become more westernized, collectivistic social rela- tions and values that are represented in house styles shift to individualistic forms (83).

findings.antecedent: living in a more rectangularly shaped, "carpentered" world (Westerners)
findings.consequent: susceptibility to certain geometric optical illusions
findings.mechanism: learning conditioned by rectangular environments affects spatial perception
findings.quote: The finding that Western- ers, more often than non-Westerners, were susceptible to certain optical illusions was explained as a result of their living in a more rectangularly shaped, "carpentered" world (348).

findings.consequent: achievement of privacy through rules regulating interpersonal behavior
findings.mechanism: privacy is often managed through social rules rather than purely physical manipulation of the environment
findings.quote: he finds privacy is achieved more often through rules regulating interpersonal behavior rather than by direct manipu- lation of the environment.

findings.antecedent: linkage of psychological and physical features of the home
findings.consequent: regulation of behavior through dialectical oppositions of identity/community and openness/closedness
findings.mechanism: the interplay of psychological and physical features in the home helps regulate social behavior
findings.quote: A cross-cultural comparison of the home reveals how the linkage of psychological and physical features serves expressive ends and aids in the regulation of behavior through the dialectical oppositions of identity/community and openness/closedness (11).

findings.antecedent: changes in local practice, utilization of fields, daily life paths, and institutional projects
findings.mechanism: daily practices and institutional projects actively transform social structures over time
findings.quote: Changes in local practice, the utilization of fields, the dialectics of individual daily and life paths, and institutional projects are shown to have transformed Swedish social structure (293).

limitations: theoretical development and empirical work across these areas uneven
how people fulfill housing needs with built forms is still somewhat unclear
the processes by which decisions are made to build, remodel, or move are neither well documented nor understood in most of the societies where anthropologists have worked
the meaning of the built environment as revealed through its metaphorical connections and ritual practices constitutes an incompletely explored dimension

the analysis and interpretation of building decisions cannot be understood apart from social and economic institutional forces that continuously influence actors, nor can the interpretation of symbolic meaning be divorced from these forces or history
